Evident scanning errors are silently corrected, including in the biblical citations (e.g. Matt. 3:17 for the printed III, 47; John 17:3 for XVII, 5; John 7:16 for VII, 46; Acts 5:3, 4 for v, 5. 4). The letters (a), (b), (c) printed before sections are taken as marks of the edition and omitted. Line 1: the Psalm quotation as given lacks "from the womb" (ex utero), which the comment on the womb presupposes. Line 3: "in quo omnes homines peccaverunt" is rendered "in whom", as the argument from the one man requires, though it could be taken as "in which". "Et ira" is read as "et ita"; "a parte tutum hominem" as "a parte totum hominem". "Quod Filio sapientiae et Spiritui sancto est esse" is awkward and may be corrupt; "sapientiae" is taken loosely as describing the Son. "Sola sapientia" is taken as an ablative, "by wisdom alone".

Ch. III: 'sed ut missus' at the opening looks faulty; the sense taken is 'how he is said to have been sent'. The garbled 'sril cct quin' is read as a phrase meaning 'except in that' or 'but because'. 'Iussus' is read as 'missus', 'Iaculi. nis' as 'locutionis', and 'a tequainGant' as 'antequam fiant'. The sentence 'Quia persona divinitatis suae assumpta est...' seems corrupt and is translated as it stands; the sense expected is that his humanity was assumed into the person of his divinity, and 'unitatem habitumque' is obscure. Ch. IV: the printed reference 'VII, 59' is corrected to John 7:39. 'sed si manet in eis' is abrupt and the text may be faulty. Ch. V: 'non unius ejusdemque substantiae' runs against the argument, which needs 'of one and the same substance'; 'non' may be corrupt (perhaps for 'nonne'). In the lamp simile, 'quo sine lucernae igne pervenit ignis' is awkward and probably corrupt; the expected sense is that the brightness reaches the wall where the fire itself does not. A printed footnote has been scanned into the middle of the sentence 'Qui me autem misit, mecum est' and is omitted from the translation. It says that the copyist shamefully disfigures the sentence, and that what follows is only excerpts from Augustine's book Against the Sermon of the Arians, badly patched together, with sentences cut short or interpolated.

This stretch is not part of the preceding work: it is the printed edition's editorial notice introducing the next book, and the reference 'col. 1208, cap. 2' is to that edition. 'Victorino' is taken to mean a manuscript of the abbey of Saint-Victor in Paris. Evident scanning errors corrected: 'qua' to 'quae', 'el' to 'et', 'ei' to 'et'.

nodes.text: ON THE TRINITY AND UNITY OF GOD. One Book.

CHAPTER ONE. The beginning of Genesis clearly shows the person of the begotten Son, for it says, In the beginning God made heaven and earth (Gen. 1:1). Whom else do we think is to be understood as the beginning, if not the Son? For when the Jews asked him who he was, he himself answered concerning himself, The beginning, who am also speaking to you (John 8:25). Therefore the Son is the beginning. Through the Son God made heaven and earth, as John the evangelist relates: All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made (John 1:3). The Son of God is Son by nature, not by adoption, as it is written: Before the morning star I begot you (Ps. 109:3). God the Father does not have a womb as we do, nor is he to be believed to be corporeal; but by "womb" he wished [us] to understand the substance from which the Son was born. What the Father is, this he begot: God [begot] God, light [begot] light, just as a man begets a man and a dog a dog. It has never been seen that a man should beget a dog. And for this reason the Father begot the Son not from nothing, nor from some other substance, but from himself.

Right faith declares the Holy Spirit to be neither unbegotten nor begotten: because if we say unbegotten, we will seem to affirm two fathers; but if begotten, we are blamed for believing in two sons. But what sure faith holds is that he is neither unbegotten nor begotten, but proceeding from both, that is, from the Father and from the Son. And so that we may prove this by testimonies, hear our Lord Jesus Christ himself saying to the disciples: When the Paraclete comes, he says, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness concerning me (John 15:26). And again the Lord Jesus Christ himself, after his resurrection, to show that the Holy Spirit proceeds from him just as from the Father, breathing on his disciples, said: Receive the Holy Spirit (John 20:22). There is therefore one Spirit of the Father and of the Son, one Spirit of both. Now, that he is the Spirit of the Father, our Lord and Savior himself says to his disciples: For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you (Matt. 10:20). And that the same is also the Spirit of the Son, the apostle Paul is witness: But if anyone, he says, does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his (Rom. 8:9).

CHAPTER II. Without doubt, in the name "God" the Father is to be understood, and in the name "beginning" the Son. Indeed, when he had said, In the beginning God made heaven and earth, he went on to add, And the Spirit of God was borne above the waters (Gen. 1:1, 2): who is the third person in the Trinity. Therefore, if there were not a threefold person, our Lord Jesus Christ would never have said to his disciples, Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matt. 28:19). Nor, when the Lord was baptized by John in the Jordan, would a voice have come from heaven, saying: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased (Matt. 3:17). Nor would the Holy Spirit be said to have descended upon him in the form of a dove, and to have remained. Therefore, in accordance with the holy Scriptures, we understand three persons, that is, that the Father is one [person], the Son, who was begotten by the Father, another, and the Holy Spirit another: not another thing, because in substance they are one. We distinguish the persons; we do not divide the deity. Now, that the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are of one substance the blessed apostle Paul demonstrates, writing to the Romans about the Son: Whose are the fathers, he says, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed for ever (Rom. 9:5). And again in the Gospel according to John, That they may know you, the only true one God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent (John 17:3): that is, you and Jesus Christ whom you have sent, the true one God. And again Scripture says, That we may be in his true Son Jesus Christ; he is true God and eternal life (1 John 5:20). And to show his equality, the Lord himself says, I and the Father are one (John 10:30): that is, in nature, not in person. And again it says, For this reason the Jews sought to kill Jesus, because he not only broke the sabbath, but also called God his Father, making himself equal to God (John 5:18). And again Paul says, Who, though he was in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal to God (Phil. 2:6). There could be no robbery where the nature was equal; it was not usurped but born; he did not seize it, because he truly had it. That the Holy Spirit is God, the Acts of the Apostles teaches most openly: Ananias, says Peter, why has Satan tempted your heart, that you should lie to the Holy Spirit? And below, You have not lied to men but to God (Acts 5:3, 4). And in the Gospel according to John it says: The Lord is spirit (John 4:24). Paul, writing to the Corinthians, says: Do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God, and that you are not your own? The same Paul: For you were bought at a great price; glorify and carry God in your body (1 Cor. 6:19, 20). The Father, I say, is God, the Son is God, the Holy Spirit is God: not three gods, but there is one God, as Moses says: Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God (Deut. 6:4). And for this reason, just as we speak not of three gods and not of three essences, so neither [do we speak] of three wisdoms nor of three spirits. For when asked about the individual persons, whether the Father is wisdom, or the Son, or the Holy Spirit, we answer: the Father is wisdom, the Son is wisdom, the Holy Spirit is wisdom: not three wisdoms, nor three spirits, but one wisdom and one spirit, just as [there is] one substance and one essence: because for that Father to be is the same as for the Son, [who is] wisdom, and for the Holy Spirit to be. And although the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are equal, the Son nevertheless says, The Father is greater than I (John 14:28); and, I did not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me (John 6:38, 40); and, Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me (Matt. 26:39); and, My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me (John 7:16). All these things, and others that the Son says, are to be understood and were said according to the form of a servant which he assumed. So then, when the first man had been created by God and endowed with free will, and a command had been laid on him that, if he kept what God had commanded him, he should not die by the death of body or of soul, he nevertheless, disobedient to the command of God and lifted up by pride, obeying the persuasion of the serpent, despised the commandments. And this was the reason why he incurred the danger of death; and from that one man all human nature, corrupted and liable to sin, became mortal. Hence the apostle Paul says, Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death: and so death passed through to all men, in whom all men sinned. For just as through one man all men fell into condemnation, so also through the justice of one all men have risen to the justice of life (Rom. 5:12, 18); and again, The first man, from the earth, was earthly; the second man, from heaven, is heavenly (1 Cor. 15:47). I call him heavenly, then, because he was not conceived from human seed, but was assumed from the virgin Mary, for our salvation, by the Son of God, as John testifies: And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us (John 1:14). The Word was made flesh, not changed into flesh so as to cease to be what he was, but he began to be what he was not: for he took flesh, he did not turn into flesh. By this flesh we understand, from the part, the whole man, that is, flesh and a rational soul: so that, as the first man had died in both flesh and soul, so too it was necessary that through the Mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus, he should be brought to life in both flesh and soul. Therefore, as we said above, it was according to the form of the flesh he assumed that it was said, The Father is greater than I (John 14:28). It must not be believed that the Son of God and the Son of man can be two sons; for they are not two sons, but one. For he who was the Son of God became the son of man in unity of person. As soul and flesh are one man, so the Word and man are one Christ. We accept two substances in the one Son of God, one of deity, the other of humanity, not two persons. And if we say two persons, we will also introduce two sons of God, and then there will no longer be a Trinity, but a quaternity; which God forbid. For indeed, by that which he is as God, he is both equal to the Father and present everywhere, and he is whole in heaven and whole on earth, and is contained in no place: by that which he is as man, he both suffered and died, and rose and ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the Father, and will come thus to judge the living and the dead, just as he was seen to go into heaven, in the same form and substance of flesh; to which he indeed gave immortality, but whose nature he did not take away. Although there is one substance, neither the person of the Father nor [that] of the Holy Spirit, but that of the Son alone took on flesh. And so that we may understand this, I will use comparisons. Surely (so that you may understand the Creator from the creature) reason is in the soul in such a way that, though they are one, the soul does one thing and reason another; by the soul we live, by reason we are wise: so the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, though they are one substance, the whole Trinity wrought the man whom not the whole Trinity assumed, but the person of the Son alone. The Father begot the Son neither by will nor by necessity. Not by necessity, because there is no necessity in God; not by will, because will cannot go before wisdom, which is the Son. For to be wise rationally comes before willing rationally. Hence the Father begot the Son neither by will nor by necessity, but naturally, by wisdom alone. As the Father has life in himself, so he has given to the Son to have life in himself (John 5:26). We know that the Son of God is not from himself, but begotten of the Father; but that the Father was begotten by no one, and received life from no one. The Father gave life to the Son by begetting the life which the Father had in himself. Not that the Son was previously without life and afterwards received life, as we, who lost life through sin, have received life back through the grace of the Savior. It is said of him, then, that the Son received life from the Father, because he was not begotten by himself: he did not give [it] to one already existing, but by begetting.

CHAPTER III. Since we have persuaded [you], both by argument and by testimonies, concerning the subjection of the Son, that he is less not according to substance but according to the form of a servant which he assumed, we now wish to say something about how he is said to have been sent. We know that just as the Son is not said to be sent, or less, according to substance, so too the Holy Spirit is not said to be sent on account of the dove or the fire, except in that he appeared not in that substance in which he is equal to the Father, but, as has been said, through a subject creature. For the Holy Spirit did not assume the dove or the fire in the way that the Son assumed a man, so as to remain forever; rather, those visions, made from lower creation in order to manifest the Spirit, afterwards ceased to exist. For that incomprehensible and immutable divinity, which is God the Trinity, can never be seen by fleshly eyes except, as has been said, through a subject creature. Between the begotten Son and the procession of the Holy Spirit there is this difference, that the Son of God is from the Father as one born, not as one given, whereas the Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son not as one born, but as one given. The Son who is born is of the Father alone, not of the Holy Spirit. The Spirit is of both, that is, of the Father and of the Son, because if the Spirit were called a son, he would be called the son of both. But no one is the son of two except of a father and a mother, and far be it that anyone should suspect this between God the Father and the Son, for not even a son of man proceeds from father and mother at the same time: when he proceeds from the father, he does not then proceed from the mother, and when he proceeds from the mother into this light, he does not then proceed also from the father. But the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Father into the Son, and from the Son proceed to sanctify creation; rather, he proceeds from both at once. Concerning what John says, that the Holy Spirit does not speak from himself, but whatever he will hear, he will speak (John 16:13): he does not speak from himself, because he is not from himself. For the Father was born of no one, the Son was begotten of the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son; therefore he does not speak from himself, but whatever he will hear, he will speak. For him, to hear is to be; he is not from himself, but from the Father; therefore whatever he will hear, he will speak. As to what it means that the Holy Spirit is said to intercede for us, as Paul says, writing to the Romans: For we do not know what we should pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself asks for us with unutterable groanings. And he who searches hearts knows what the Spirit desires, because he asks according to God for the saints (Rom. 8:26-27). This manner of speaking, which is often found in the holy Scriptures, is like God's saying to Abraham, Now I have known that you fear God (Gen. 22:12), that is, I have made you know; just as the Apostle says, Now knowing God, or rather known by God (Gal. 4:9). For surely all things are in the presence of God before they come to be; things to come are present, as though they had already been done. How does he say "known by God", unless [it means] God causing us to know God? So here too the Holy Spirit is written to groan for us, that is, to make us groan, by pouring into us love for God and neighbor; just as we read of a "glad day", because it makes people glad. The Father alone is nowhere read to have been sent, but the Apostle writes of the sending of the Son thus: But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, made under the law, to redeem those who were under the law (Gal. 4:4-5). That the Son of God, born of the Virgin Mary, came into the world, the evangelist testifies, saying, He was in the world, and the world was made through him (John 1:10). And he himself says, I went out from the Father and have come into this world (John 16:28). Likewise the evangelist says, And the world did not know him. Then he adds, He came to his own (John 1:10-11). He was surely sent to the place to which he came; but he was sent into this world, where he [already] was. Yet that this sending is the work of the Holy Trinity no Catholic should doubt. Nowhere is it written that God the Father is greater than the Holy Spirit, or the Holy Spirit less than God the Father, because it is not so. Because the person of his divinity was assumed by the Son of God from the Virgin Mary into the person of his humanity, he joined unity and condition forever. Although the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove or of fire, we still cannot call the Holy Spirit God and dove, or God and fire, as we call the Son God and man. On account of these bodily forms, then, in which the Holy Spirit appeared, he is said to be sent; he cannot on account of them be called less than the Father, as the Son is on account of the form of a servant, which clung to him perpetually in unity of person. But those bodily appearances, such as that of the dove or the fire, appeared for a time to show what was needed, and afterwards ceased to exist. Was it not right that creatures should appear as was fitting, serving the Creator at the nod of him who remains unchangeably in himself, being altered and transformed in order to signify and show him, as it was fitting that he should be signified and shown to mortals?

CHAPTER IV. Some are accustomed to doubt whether the Apostles had the Holy Spirit at the time when they were with Christ the Lord, in view of what the evangelist says: The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified (John 7:39). And in another place he says: If you love me, keep my commandments; and I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, that he may be with you forever, the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him. But you see him and know him, because he remains with you and is with you (John 14:15-17). And further, after his resurrection, he is read to have breathed on the disciples and said, Receive the Holy Spirit (John 20:22). But at Pentecost the Holy Spirit is read to have descended upon the Apostles (Acts 2:4). To these things it must be said that there is one Spirit, but he has many gifts. There is no doubt that the Holy Spirit was with them, because where Christ is, the Holy Spirit is. And because Christ had promised that the Holy Spirit would come from the Father, his undifferentiated divinity was not lacking in this. Three forms of office belonging to the gift of the Holy Spirit were shown in the Apostles. The first of them is that which pertains to ecclesiastical right, in those who are to be regenerated. Ecclesiastical power is understood to lie in the offices of bishops and priests, who must do everything in the Lord's tradition through the Holy Spirit. Hence Jesus says to them, Those whose sins you retain, they will be retained; and those whose [sins] you forgive, they will be forgiven them (John 20:23). The second is that which was given at Pentecost, which is general: for the Holy Spirit fell not only upon the Apostles, but also upon all believers. The third form is that which was granted only to the Apostles, or to those ordained at the beginning, for performing signs and mighty works, until they should cast the seeds of faith for growth. For the seeds of faith are the mighty works done through the Apostles: for the Apostles themselves were appointed as overseers of this truth, and they testify through signs and wonders that our faith is reasonable. So the Holy Spirit is given generally to all believers, but if he remains in them; and by signs and wonders they are proved to be sons of God. Moreover, the Holy Spirit does not always remain in a person, but when called he comes, to prompt what is necessary, and withdraws. Similarly also in the handing on or ordination, from outside he grants grace and protection to those devoted to the faith, that they may be held in higher regard through his inspiration.

CHAPTER V. The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one true God, according to what is written: Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God is one (Deut. 6:4). And in the Gospel it is written: That they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent (John 17:3). And of Christ the apostle John says: He is the true God and eternal life (1 John 5:20). The Son existed before all times, as is to be understood in this: In the beginning was the Word; and: All things were made through him. For time too cannot exist without some movements of creatures. And therefore we confess that times too were made through the Son, through whom all things were made; therefore without doubt the Son is begotten equal to, and coeternal with, the Father. The Son of God is said, by the will and command of the Father, to have made by his own power things heavenly and earthly, visible and invisible, bodies and spirits, from no existing things, that is, that they should exist from nothing; whereas he himself was not made from no existing things, that is, from nothing, but is God from God the Father: which fact indicates one and the same nature of the Father and the Son. The Son could not [be made] through himself, as though he had not existed before he was made, so that he himself should be the one through whom that same he was made. Further, if the Son was made through some other than the Father, who is that other, since all things were made through him, that is, through his Word? Before he made all things, he had been established as God and Lord, king and creator of all things to come, having in his nature foreknowledge of all things to come, and in making awaiting in all things the Father's command. By the will of the Father he came down from heaven and came into the world, as he himself says: For I did not come from myself, but he sent me. For the Trinity itself is one, since from him and through him and in him are all things. We say that the Son created all things at the Father's bidding, and that [this bidding] is nothing but the Word, through whom all things were made. That the Father sent the Son, who came with him, he himself testifies who says, I am not alone, because the Father is with me. Nor is the nature ever different because the Father sends and the Son is sent. A man who is a father can send a man who is his son, not of one and the same substance, since the man sent is separated from the man sending, which cannot be the case with God. But fire sends out its brightness, and the brightness cannot be separated from the fire that sends it. For when fire sends out brightness, the brightness reaches from it farther, to where the fire does not reach. Hence the brightness sent from the fire that is in a lamp could indeed truly be said [to be] on the wall, to which fire reached without the fire of the lamp. On this the Son says, He who sent me is with me (John 8:42, 16, 29): which the Son could truly say, The Father is with me. Since, therefore, this sending of the Son by the Father is altogether ineffable and cannot be grasped by anyone's thought, this too can be understood here: that he is said to have been sent by the Father in that the Son, not the Father, appeared to men in the flesh. For where is the Son sent, where he is not? And where is the wisdom of God not? etc.

[This book] has been attributed not to Augustine alone but, just as falsely, to many other authors: Ambrose, Jerome, Anselm, Bonaventure. Among the works of Jerome, however, it does not survive whole, but only as far as the words, All these things that have been said above, etc., col. 1208, ch. 2; and there it is entitled, On the Things Attributed to God in the Scriptures. Among those of Anselm, On the Garments and Limbs and Acts Attributed to God. Among those of Bonaventure, On the Essence and Invisibility and Immensity of God. In the Vatican and Saint-Victor manuscripts, under the name of Augustine, it has the title, On the Essence of the Divinity and on the Invisibility and Unchangeability of God. The first and largest part of the book, taken from the work of Eucherius of Lyon, On the Formulas of Spiritual Understanding, contains the whole first chapter of that work, which is On the Divine Names.
